title: An unchartered network of letters and hosts, from a Jerusalem nucleus to an emperor's council
register: documentary, and suspicious of its own heresiologists
summary: No Roman official ever met a chartered Christian corporation, only individuals who met in houses, sang a hymn, shared a meal, and forwarded each other's letters by whatever traveler was going the right way. What held scattered assemblies together was correspondence, hospitality, and the claim of a shared origin, carried on Roman roads and Mediterranean shipping lanes built for other purposes; what ended in 325 was not the network but its independence from the state that had been intermittently killing its members. At Nicaea an emperor, not a courier, collapsed the distance for the first time.

nodes.name: Jerusalem
nodes.note: Origin memory, the earliest leadership under Cephas, James and John, and the destination of Paul's collection for the poor. Destroyed in 70 and refounded as Aelia Capitolina after 135; it retained prestige without being the administrative capital of all Christianity.

nodes.name: Antioch-on-the-Orontes
nodes.note: The bridge between Judaean origins and gentile mission, site of the Cephas–Paul dispute over table fellowship and the point from which Ignatius was sent west under guard.

nodes.name: Damascus
nodes.note: An early community and travel junction between Syria and Arabia, secure in Paul's own letters though narrative particulars in Acts are partly uncorroborated.

nodes.name: Tarsus
nodes.note: Paul's place of origin and an east–west land and maritime junction; his origin here is secure, though the local Christian community's own internal history is sparsely documented.

nodes.name: Ephesus
nodes.note: A Pauline base, port, and regional hub for manuscript and teacher circulation in Asia, later addressed by Ignatius on his journey west.

nodes.name: Corinth-Cenchreae
nodes.note: A two-gulf port complex connecting Italy, the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean; recipient of 1 Clement from Rome and later of Dionysius's correspondence with Soter's Rome.

nodes.name: Philippi
nodes.note: A Macedonian assembly that sent remittances to Paul through Epaphroditus and, decades later, wrote to Polycarp asking for copies of Ignatius's letters.

nodes.name: Thessalonica
nodes.note: A Macedonian mission and correspondence node attested directly in Paul's letters.

nodes.name: Rome
nodes.note: An immigrant assembly before Paul's arrival, and by the second century a doctrinal market and arbitration venue precisely because it was the capital and transport hub. Its later claim to a fully centralized first-century papacy exceeds the surviving evidence.

nodes.name: Alexandria
nodes.note: Securely visible by the late second century through Pantaenus, Clement, Origen, Demetrius and Heraclas; the tradition of a first-century Markan founding cannot itself be independently confirmed.

nodes.name: Carthage
nodes.note: Secure from the Scillitan martyr acts, Tertullian and Cyprian; under Cyprian it generated the richest surviving operational correspondence of any pre-Nicene regional network, coordinating clergy, relief, councils and ransom.

nodes.name: Smyrna
nodes.note: Where Ignatius received delegations and wrote several letters under guard, and Polycarp's own base as the relay and archive for the Ignatian correspondence.

nodes.name: Caesarea Maritima
nodes.note: Origen's teaching and manuscript center after his break with Bishop Demetrius of Alexandria, later the seed of Pamphilus's library and Palestinian episcopal communication.

nodes.name: Edessa
nodes.note: A Syriac literary node on the routes toward Nisibis, Adiabene and the Iranian sphere, established by the late second or early third century through Bardaisan's milieu. The Abgar–Jesus correspondence attached to it later is a foundation legend, not contemporary evidence.

nodes.name: Nicomedia
nodes.note: Site of Pliny's early-second-century inquiry into accused Christians and, in 303, of a conspicuous church near the imperial palace demolished at the opening of the Great Persecution.

nodes.name: Nicaea
nodes.note: The temporary convergence point for an empire-wide episcopal council, some 200 to 300 bishops, summoned and subsidized by Constantine: the moment the network became reachable by imperial logistics rather than only by its own couriers.

nodes.name: Lyons
nodes.note: Recipient community of an Asian-migrant congregation whose martyr letter, addressed to Asia and Phrygia, is direct evidence that the Rhône corridor was tied to Asia Minor; Irenaeus embodied the same connection in person.

nodes.name: Dura-Europos
nodes.note: The best-preserved pre-Constantinian Christian meeting complex, with a decorated baptistery; its precise architectural category is disputed, but the Christian identification is secure. The city fell to the Sasanians in 256.

nodes.name: Numidia
nodes.note: Where local bishops reported Christians taken captive, prompting Carthage to raise and send a ransom fund; a recurring correspondent in Cyprian's regional network of councils and disputes.

nodes.name: Paul
nodes.note: The best-documented itinerant organizer, founding and maintaining assemblies through manual work, coworkers and letters rather than administering territorial dioceses. His letters, not Acts, are the earliest surviving Christian documents; his death under Nero is traditional rather than contemporaneously narrated.

nodes.name: Ignatius of Antioch
nodes.note: Bishop transported under guard from Antioch toward Rome, writing letters at Smyrna and Troas that Polycarp then collected and forwarded: the clearest early example of correspondence becoming a distributed archive. His exact travel date is disputed within a roughly 107–117 range.

nodes.name: Polycarp
nodes.note: Bishop of Smyrna who collected and forwarded Ignatius's letters to Philippi and remembered by Irenaeus as a personal, near-filial connection between Asia Minor and Gaul.

nodes.name: Cyprian of Carthage
nodes.note: Bishop whose surviving correspondence, over eighty letters, is the richest operational record of any pre-Nicene regional network: episcopal disputes, the lapsi controversy, and the Numidian ransom collection. Executed in 258 under Valerian.

nodes.name: Origen
nodes.note: Moved from Alexandria to Caesarea after conflict with Bishop Demetrius, building a teaching and manuscript center there. Traveled to Rome and Arabia and was summoned to a synod addressing Beryllus of Bostra; died from injuries sustained under the Decian persecution.

nodes.name: Dionysius of Corinth
nodes.note: Wrote to Athens, Sparta, Nicomedia, Crete, Pontus and Rome, and thanked the Roman church and its bishop Soter for charitable aid. His letters survive only through Eusebius's later excerpts.

nodes.name: Marcion
nodes.note: Assembled a gospel-and-apostle collection in Rome that forced or accelerated debate over authoritative Christian books; his donation to the Roman church and his subsequent break with it are known chiefly through hostile later report.

nodes.name: Bardaisan
nodes.note: His school produced the Syriac Book of the Laws of Countries, whose reference to Christians in Edessa, Persia, Media, Parthia and among the Geli is genuine early evidence, though rhetorical generalization cannot establish the size of any one community.

nodes.name: Phoebe of Cenchreae
nodes.note: Called diakonos of the church at Cenchreae and prostatis of many including Paul; plausibly, though not explicitly stated, the carrier of Paul's letter to the Roman assemblies. Direct evidence of a woman entrusted with translocal standing.

nodes.name: Prisca and Aquila
nodes.note: A mobile married pair expelled from Rome under Claudius, appearing afterward in Corinth and Ephesus and later again in Rome. Their craft and household supplied economic and meeting infrastructure everywhere they went, including instruction of Apollos.

nodes.name: Pliny the Younger
nodes.note: As governor, interrogated accused Christians, found a regular meeting, a hymn to Christ, an oath and a common meal, and tortured two enslaved ministrae for information. Trajan's rescript in reply is an administrative response to a local problem, not a charter for or against Christianity empire-wide.

nodes.name: Emperor Decius
nodes.note: Ordered empire-wide sacrifice and certification in 249/250; the edict itself is lost, but surviving Egyptian libelli document the bureaucratic transaction. Christians were disproportionately endangered because many refused to comply.

nodes.name: Emperor Diocletian
nodes.note: Ordered the first Great Persecution edict from Nicomedia in 303: churches demolished, scriptures burned, officeholders degraded. Enforcement varied by emperor, province and date; he abdicated in 305 with the persecution still underway elsewhere.

nodes.name: Emperor Constantine
nodes.note: Co-issued the 313 toleration measure conventionally called the Edict of Milan, restoring Christian corporate property, then summoned and subsidized the empire-wide council at Nicaea in 325, attaching the network to treasury, court and coercive enforcement for the first time.

nodes.name: The Jerusalem collection
nodes.note: Paul's fundraising drive among gentile assemblies for impoverished believers in Jerusalem, meant to bind newly founded communities materially to the movement's Judaean origin. No surviving total is given for the amount raised.

nodes.name: Cyprian's Numidian ransom fund
nodes.note: 100,000 sesterces raised in Carthage from clergy and laity, men and women, after Numidian bishops reported Christians taken captive: one of the only quantified pre-Nicene financial transfers to survive.

nodes.name: The Ignatian letter archive
nodes.note: The seven middle-recension letters Ignatius wrote at Smyrna and Troas, collected by Polycarp and copied onward to Philippi at Philippi's own request: documented early evidence of Christian correspondence becoming a duplicated, forwarded archive rather than a single point-to-point delivery.
